title: The Little Shop of Horrors

evidence.note: Wikipedia reports that Corman did not believe the film had much financial prospect after its initial theatrical run, so he did not bother to copyright it, and the film entered the public domain. It gives a release date of September 14, 1960. This is a secondary source. No Catalog of Copyright Entries page, Copyright Office record or notice-failure document was fetched. Other web claims about a later registration or a lapsed renewal were not confirmed and conflict with the 'never copyrighted' account, so the print is not marked verified.

evidence.note: Wikipedia credits the score to cellist Fred Katz, with Ronald Stein uncredited. This is a sound film, so the recorded track would normally share the film's own copyright status. No registration for the music was checked, so its status is not confirmed.

evidence.note: Wikipedia credits the screenplay to Charles B. Griffith. Its status follows the film's. The 1982 stage musical and 1986 film are separate derivative works, and their songs and book are not covered by anything said here about the 1960 film.

evidence.note: The title is also used by a licensed stage-musical franchise. Avoid using it as branding for products or shows. No trademark registration was checked.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright: copying or restoring public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). What a restoration ADDS can be protected: a newly composed or newly recorded score, colorization, newly written or translated titles and subtitles, and other original additions. Separately, ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD can break the DMCA's anti-circumvention rule (17 U.S.C. 1201) even when the film itself is public domain.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp. (summary)

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. 1201 - circumvention of copyright protection systems.
Colorized versions and modern restorations are separately protected.

editorial:
Roger Corman directed and produced The Little Shop of Horrors, released September 14, 1960 and distributed by The Filmgroup and American International Pictures, from a screenplay by Charles B. Griffith. Jonathan Haze, Jackie Joseph and Mel Welles lead the cast, with Jack Nicholson in a supporting role. The music is credited to cellist Fred Katz, with Ronald Stein uncredited. A creator might want it as a short, quotable horror comedy about a man and his carnivorous plant.

Wikipedia reports that Corman did not think the film had much financial prospect after its initial theatrical run, so he did not copyright it, and the film entered the public domain. That is a secondary account. No primary record is attached here, and other web sources give conflicting stories about registration and renewal, so the print stays Undetermined. The rights trap is the franchise built on top of it. The 1982 stage musical and the 1986 film are separate derivative works, so their songs and book are not covered by the 1960 film's status. The title is also used by a licensed musical franchise, so avoid it as branding.
faq: Can I use the songs from Little Shop of Horrors?
Not on the strength of the 1960 film. The songs come from the 1982 musical and 1986 film, which are separate derivative works. They are not covered by anything said here about the 1960 original.

It is widely reported to be public domain because it was never copyrighted, but this dossier has no primary record, so the print stays Undetermined. If you rely on it, keep your own evidence. Do not assume that a particular restored copy, added score or colorized version is free.
